Ground Friday 10:00 to 10:45 Great Hall

Maintenanceas a public act.

Forty five minutes on why the work that keeps a thing running is almost never the work anybody is given credit for, and what changes when it is written down in public.

Given by

Ruth Pellamy

An invented speaker. This page is an example of what a talk page in this edition looks like.

01

What the talk covers

A pumping station is a good place to think about maintenance, because a pumping station that is working looks exactly like a pumping station that nobody is looking after. The difference only appears later, and by then it is expensive.

This talk works through three illustrative examples: a register of parts that was kept by one person for eleven years, a drainage map that was redrawn every time somebody joined the team, and a rota that nobody wrote down because everybody knew it. Two of those survived a change of staff. One did not.

A thing that is maintained in private looks identical to a thing that is not maintained at all.

The second half turns to what changes when maintenance is done where people can see it: what gets easier, what gets slower, and which of the arguments against working in the open turn out to be arguments about something else entirely.

There is no slide deck. Questions are taken for the last ten minutes, and the room is cleared straight afterwards because the next session in the Great Hall starts at 11:00.

02

About the speaker

Every speaker in this edition is invented. Replace the biography, the sessions and the link before publishing.

Ruth Pellamy works on the parts of public systems that nobody photographs: registers, rotas, spare part lists and the handover notes that sit between one person leaving and the next one starting. She has spent most of the last decade arguing that these are the documents worth publishing.

She opens the Sunday morning session as well, and will be in the courtyard for most of Friday afternoon.
